items.paragraph: It is sometimes said that a politician who lies to the public or bargains with a ruthless faction to prevent a greater harm has simply done the right thing, and that once the calculation favours the act, no moral residue remains. This tidy view misdescribes the situation. The act may be justified, all things considered, and still involve doing something wrong: deceiving people who were owed the truth, or lending strength to people who deserved none. A leader who felt nothing after such a choice would be more worrying than one who felt the weight of it, because that weight is how a person registers that a real claim was overridden rather than dissolved. Justification answers whether one should act; it does not erase what the act cost those it wronged.

items.paragraph: Historians have learned to read archives not only for what they say but for what they leave out. An archive is the residue of an administration's interests: it keeps tax rolls, court cases and correspondence among officials, and so it records people mainly when they paid, offended or petitioned. Whole areas of life, such as household work, friendship and private belief, appear only when they collided with authority. It has become common to conclude that the archive simply silences the powerless. That conclusion goes too far. The same court records that reduce a person to a defendant often preserve, in the words of witnesses, details of daily life recorded nowhere else, and a petition written to flatter an official can still reveal what its writer wanted. The archive is biased in what it selects, but read against its grain it yields more about ordinary lives than its makers ever intended.

items.paragraph: A popular answer to the question of what makes someone the same person over time is memory: I am the person who did the things I can remember doing. That repair helps, but it quietly concedes the original point: it is not remembering that makes me the same person, but something continuous of which remembering is only one part.

items.paragraph: A familiar account of why great empires fall points to overextension: they conquer more territory than they can defend or administer, and the cost of holding distant frontiers drains the centre. items.paragraph: Making a machine more efficient seems an obvious way to reduce the energy it consumes, but economists have long noted an awkward complication. When a service becomes cheaper to run, people tend to use more of it: a more economical car makes longer journeys affordable, and cheaper lighting invites more of it. Some of the expected saving is therefore taken back in additional use. It does not follow, as enthusiasts of the idea sometimes conclude, that efficiency is futile. Whether the rebound swallows a small or a large part of the saving depends on how much more of the service people actually want once its price falls, and for many household uses that appetite is limited; nobody keeps the fridge door open because the fridge is economical. The finding is a reason to estimate savings honestly, not a reason to abandon the pursuit of them.

items.paragraph: Two accounts of medieval craft guilds have long competed. items.paragraph: Languages that oblige speakers to choose between a familiar and a respectful form of 'you' are sometimes thought more hierarchical than those, like modern English, that use a single form for everyone. The comparison is misleading. Speakers of English mark distance and rank in other ways: through first names or titles, through how directly they make requests, through who may start a conversation and who may end it. A language without the grammatical choice has not abolished the social one; it has moved it elsewhere, often to places where it is harder for a newcomer to notice. If anything, the explicit pronoun makes the rules of respect easier to see and therefore easier to learn.

items.paragraph: Moral philosophers often test principles against imagined cases: a runaway trolley, a surgeon with five dying patients, a drowning child beside an expensive suit. The method is defended on the ground that stripping away messy detail isolates the feature that matters. But the stripping is not neutral. A real surgeon could never be certain that the transplant would succeed, that no one would find out, or that the healthy visitor had no one depending on him; our reluctance to approve the killing may be a sound response to exactly these uncertainties, which the case asks us to set aside but which our intuitions were formed to track. When an intuition about an idealised case conflicts with a principle, it is therefore unclear which has been refuted. This does not make imagined cases useless, since they can still show that a principle has implications its defenders had not noticed; it makes them weaker as evidence against principles than they are usually taken to be.

items.paragraph: Schools that pair older pupils with younger ones for tutoring usually set out to help the younger children, and they often do. A recurring observation, however, is that the tutors gain as much or more: having to explain an idea to someone who does not yet grasp it forces the tutor to organise what he or she half knows, to notice gaps and to find examples. This benefit is not automatic. A tutor who merely supplies answers, or who is given material far below his or her own level with no need to explain it, gains little. The gain comes from the effort of explanation, and schools that want it must design tutoring so that explanation is actually required.

items.paragraph: Coins are usually studied as tools of exchange, but for many early states they were just as much instruments of announcement. A ruler's face on a coin travelled to markets the ruler would never visit, carried by people who might never see a proclamation or a soldier. Every transaction quietly repeated the claim that this authority stood behind the value in one's hand. That is one reason why new regimes so often hurried to strike their own coins, even when the old ones worked perfectly well as money. To read coins only for their weight and purity is to miss half of what they were for.

items.paragraph: It is often said that there is no disputing about taste, and in one sense this is right: no argument will make someone enjoy a dish they find bitter. Yet people argue about taste constantly, and not pointlessly. When a friend explains what to listen for in a piece of music, or why a film's slow opening earns its later payoff, she is not trying to overrule my pleasure by decree. She is directing my attention to features I may have missed, so that my next response is better informed. Such arguments cannot compel agreement, but they can change what there is to respond to. Taste is not beyond reason; it is simply reached by reasons of a different kind, ones that work by showing rather than by proving.

items.paragraph: Coral gardening, in which fragments are grown in underwater nurseries and then fixed onto damaged reefs, has become the most visible form of reef restoration, and its photographs of divers planting coral are genuinely encouraging. Yet its scale should be kept in view. A well-run project may replant a few hectares, while the reefs being lost to warming seas are measured in thousands of square kilometres, and transplanted corals die in the next marine heatwave as readily as wild ones. None of this makes the work pointless: nurseries can preserve heat-tolerant strains and keep particular reefs alive for tourism or fisheries. But treating gardening as a solution to reef decline mistakes a holding action for a cure, since only reducing the warming itself addresses the cause.
